Our study area is mainly located in a forest mosaic landscape comprised by woodlands, grasslands, farmlands, and bare ground during the vegetation growing season on the south bank of this river. [prose] Three ecological traits that characterised functional diversity between ground beetle species included: body size (large vs. small), feeding trait (carnivorous vs. omnivorous), and wing morphology (macropterous vs. brachypterous) (Homburg et al., 2014) (Supporting Information Table S1). Body length was used as a measure of body size, which was measured as the distance from the tip of the mandibles to the end of the abdomen. Carabid species with an average body size equal to or longer than 15 mm were considered large; otherwise, they were considered small (Gobbi et al., 2007). Carabid species were considered carnivorous if they were strictly predators during their life cycle, whereas species that were occasional predators or herbivores were considered omnivorous (Gobbi & Fontaneto, 2008). For wing morphology, macropterous species were those with wings longer than the elytra, whereas brachypterous species were those with wings shorter than the elytra (Brambilla & Gobbi, 2014). As DBH is often used as a proxy of tree height in most tree species, we only considered DBH as measure of tree size, which is an important structural trait, critical in forest ecology and for above ground biomass estimate. Canopy cover was assessed at four continuous 10 m  10 m assessment areas along the transect using a visual cover method (Humphrey et al., 1999). Percentage of vegetation cover on each plot was calculated from 10 random $1 \; \mathrm { { m } } \times 1$ m quadrats along the transect (Rahman et al., 2015). We also measured species richness and average height of herbaceous plant species in three random $5 \mathrm { ~ m ~ } \times 5$ m sampling subplots within each sampling plot. An important environmental factor, the nearest distance from the centre of sampling plot to river bank (the distance to river, Magagula, 2003; Rykken et al., 2007) was measured by using ENVI version 5.4 based on satellite images.

[prose] Landscape structure of surrounding vegetation was measured in a 300 m radius buffer (Wang et al., 2019). The geographical coordinates of the centre of each sampling plot were collected using a handheld GPS unit. Then, based on these coordinates, open-access remote sensing images were acquired on 28 June 2018 for the whole study area covering six villages from the European ‘Sentinel-2A’ satellite. We preprocessed remote sensing images using ENVI version 5.4 software in order to eliminate errors and improve their quality, including radiation correction and atmospheric correction. The results of image-interpretation were rectified by adequate ground-truth data recorded in a forest vegetation survey. The normalised difference vegetation index (NDVI) is often used as a preferred surrogate for vegetation productivity of the terrestrial ecosystems (Voepel et al., 2011; Lezama et $a l .$ , 2014), particularly in applications involving land-cover change. Vegetation productivity was thus quantified by calculating NDVI values, which is defined as: $\mathrm{NDVI} = \left( \mathrm{R_{NIR}} - \mathrm{R_{red}} \right) / \left( \mathrm{R_{NIR}} + \mathrm{R_{red}} \right)$ , where R NIR and $\mathbf { R _ { r e d } }$ refer to the reflectance values derived from spectral radiances measured by the near-infrared channel and the red visible channel, respectively. NDVI values range from 1 (water) to 1 (maximum vegetation signal). We calculated NDVI values for each of 300 m radius buffers around sampling plots using ‘Band Math’ tool in ENVI version 5.4 software applied to the remote sensing image and classified NDVI values into five vegetation classes representing the intensity of the vegetation signal: (i) low vegetation (1.00 to 0.11); (ii) medium-low vegetation (0.11–0.21); (iii medium vegetation (0.21–0.51); (iv) medium-high vegetation (0.51–0.81); and (vi) high vegetation signal (0.81–1.00) (Fig. 1c). We distinguished each vegetation class based on a variation range examination of how NDVI values change in each habitat type (e.g. bare ground, shrubland, grassland, woodland, or farmland) across time. These vegetation productivity classes defined different habitat patches that had similar vegetation growth characteristics, for instance, NDVI values below 0.2 typically represent very low vegetation signal or bare ground. Using five classes enabled us to separate the amount of each vegetation productivity class during the growing season precisely (Macfadyen et al., 2015). Finally, the proportion of each of the five vegetation productivity classes was calculated in a buffer of 300 m radius centred on each sampling plot. Shannon’s Diversity Index (SHDI) was also calculated by using Fragstats version 4.2 to quantify the overall diversity of vegetation productivity classes.
